text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Nokia and Motorola competing for contract to build a billion radio communications network for Finnish authorities.

- Future digital technology may force state broadcaster YLE to seek new forms of financing, and if current funds from commercial channels dry up it may start broadcasting commercials, managing director Arne Wessberg says. @
- More flexibility in working conditions by changing law on employment contracts would have no impact on jobs situation, working group says.
- Finland faces greater economic uncertainties outside a single European currency than in it, goverment's draft position on EMU says.
- Finland should have a separate permanent representative to NATO, says Defence Minister Anneli Taina.
- A proposal to shorten working hours would increase pay costs and so destroy jobs, said Kalevi Kahri, chairman of the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT). @
KAUPPALEHTI
- Finnish paper wholesaler Amerpap plans to increase its share in paper and cardboard markets in Russia and the Baltic countries, CEO Markku Tynelli said.
- Mid-sized exporters want to be able to vary depreciation depending on yearly profits, as a competitive shield in EMU.
- Restaurant sector is boosting and employment is improving, the Hotel and Restaurant Workers' Union (HRHL) says.
- Finns with apartment loans have repaid a big chunk of their debts, bankers at Postipankki say. @
- Alfred Berg has lost its leading market share in Finland, and company's top figures plan to resign.
AAMULEHTI
- President Ahtisaari, visiting South Africa, promised to play a role of a spokesman for Africa in the future.
- Finnair pledges tough response to disturbances during flights.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Exports of high technology still rose rapidly in the first quarter of 1997. @
- OECD to hold a conference on electronics goods trade in Turku next November.
DEMARI
- Claims that Finns have become estranged from politics are not true; they are interested but not that active, political science researchers Heikki Paloheimo and Matti Wiberg say.
-- Nora Hallberg, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 292
